rows: Your two eyes together very likely cover close to a full circle. A rabbit in the freeze position has a field of 360 degrees, and only a 24 degree wedge in front is seen by both eyes at once.
You have a blue-sensitive cone that peaks near 465 nanometers and a green-sensitive cone that peaks near 509. Two kinds of cone make you a dichromat, and your rods are a third kind of light sensor.

In dim light your rods take over. Recordings from rod-fed cells in the rabbit retina peak near 500 nanometers, so you very likely see a dim scene in one blue-green gray. If you are a European rabbit, no reflecting layer sits behind your retina to give light a second pass.
A level band across your retina is the sharpest part. Cones there reach about 18,000 per square millimeter, against about 7,000 in the upper retina, and you have no fovea.

Neighboring edge-detecting ganglion cells sit 30 to 40 micrometers apart along your streak, and 1.9 micrometers of retina spans 46 arcseconds. You very likely resolve about 2 cycles per degree there, a fourteenth of the 30 a human reads on an eye chart.
You move your eyes in jumps that average about 21 degrees and are never smaller than 1 degree. When you follow something that moves, you follow it in jumps and never smoothly.
Cells in your retina answer to movement in one direction and stay quiet for the opposite one. Four kinds prefer up, down, toward the nose and toward the temple.
Nobody has measured how fast sharpness fades above and below your streak, how strongly movement stands out, or the light level at which rods take over from cones. We chose those values.
Nobody has measured some parts of how you see, so they are guesses.

This view is a guess that hasn’t yet been checked against research. A rabbit probably sees almost all the way around itself, most sharply along the horizon, in little detail, with two kinds of colour-sensing cells.
On this trial the colours come from the measured receptor peaks (425, 523 nm). The camera's colours and the display are the app's.
Nuboer, van Nuys and Wortel 1983, wild rabbit
As the light falls, the colours drift toward what the rods take in, which peak near 498 nm. The peak is measured; where the change happens is the app's guess.
